title: Local error correction prolongs time-crystalline memory
abstract: Discrete time crystals are non-equilibrium phases of matter with spatiotemporal order and a response that breaks the time-translation symmetry of a periodic external drive. Interactions, spatial disorder and correlated random driving can in theory stabilize this order. In experiments, however, coupling to the environment limits the time crystal lifetime. Here we use stochastic local bit-flip error correction to prolong the time-crystalline response of a driven, spatially disordered two-dimensional Ising model on a superconducting quantum processor, using a repetition code with distances three and five on a honeycomb lattice with up to 68 physical qubits. Even though ancilla qubits, midcircuit syndrome measurements and decoding increase the required quantum and classical resources, the stochastic drive increases the memory decay time by a factor of up to two. At late times we observe that recovery stabilizes spatial order across the lattice. The spin-configuration distributions explain this separation, as recovery suppresses disagreeing bonds while broadening occupies completely reversed states. Syndrome measurements without correction accelerate the memory decay, demonstrating the importance of conditional correction. Our results show that local bit-flip error correction can preserve time-crystalline memory over more drive cycles than the bare dynamics.
summary: This work demonstrates that applying local bit-flip error correction protocols can substantially extend the memory time of time-crystalline order in a noisy quantum simulation. By implementing recovery codes on a superconducting processor, the researchers successfully combat environmental decoherence, showing that the stabilization of spatial order is particularly pronounced. This highlights the utility of QEC techniques for preserving fragile, non-equilibrium quantum states.
main_problem: The primary goal is to extend the memory time of time-crystalline order in a noisy quantum processor by implementing local error correction protocols.
main_result: Local bit-flip error correction significantly prolongs the time-crystalline memory decay time, with five-site recovery showing the greatest enhancement compared to bare dynamics.
method: The study uses superconducting quantum processors to simulate a driven Ising model, applying stochastic local bit-flip error correction via repetition codes and syndrome measurements.
model_or_system: The system is a driven, spatially disordered two-dimensional Ising model simulated on a superconducting quantum processor using a honeycomb lattice. The dynamics are governed by a Floquet Hamiltonian incorporating disorder and external driving.
key_observables: Temporal memory decay ($	au$), spatial alignment ($A_Z$), connected correlation function ($G_c(d, n)$), and quantum negativity ($\mathcal{N}$).
important_parameters: Error correction distances (three-site and five-site), block activation probability ($p$), and the driving strength ($g$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to perform syndrome measurements and conditional recovery gates, and uses quenched disorder realizations.
figures_summary: Figures compare spatial alignment and connected correlations between bare evolution and recovery methods; Figure 2 shows temporal memory loss; Figure 4 tracks the domain-wall fraction $D(n)$ dependence on $p$.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical model and error correction implementation, presents quantitative measurements of memory decay and spatial order, and compares the performance of different recovery schemes against the bare noisy dynamics.
why_interesting: It directly addresses the crucial challenge of decoherence in simulating non-equilibrium quantum phases, providing a concrete demonstration of how quantum error correction can stabilize complex quantum memory effects.
